newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China bid to join WTO makes little headway.
newsitem.headline: China bid to join WTO makes little headway.

text.p: The European Union appeared to make little headway on Tuesday in efforts to persuade its main trading partners to jump-start stalled talks on China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan had hoped that a meeting he called of the Quad group -- the European Union, the United States, Canada and Japan -- would send a powerful political signal that it was time for the talks to resume in earnest.
But after the meeting, held during the inaugural ministerial meeting of the WTO, Brittan said the Quad had done little more than compare notes.
"We exchanged views but we did not come to a formal conclusion," he said.
Brittan set out his argument for what he called a "phased accession" to the 128-strong WTO, which would give China time to open its rapidly growing economy to the world.

But acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Washington stood by its insistence that China, which has built up a huge trade surplus with the United States, could join only on what she called commercial terms.
"The views of the administration haven't changed," she said.

"They are views that have been conveyed to the Chinese consistently and repeatedly. As we have said, we would welcome their admission to the WTO -- that is good for China, it is good for the United States and the world community -- but only on a commercially meaningful basis," Barshefsky said.

Canada was also lukewarm about Brittan's proposal. International Trade Minister Art Eggleton said Canada was willing to be flexible and to discuss the idea of a phased entry for China, but he added: "we certainly expect that China is going to meet the same rules and obligations that we are."
China said on Tuesday it was fully qualified to enter the WTO but that some unnamed western countries were blocking it.
"These obstacles are mainly due to political reasons and the excessive demands placed on China," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing in Beijing.

China has been pushing to enter the WTO on the favourable terms granted to developing nations, but many Western countries, most notably the United States, insist China's economy is too large for such treatment.
Barshefsky said the United States, like Europe, was ready to work intensively with China on membership terms.
"But ultimately entry into the WTO must be based upon conditions consistent with the WTO," she added.
Brittan, who reported on what he called very positive recent meetings with Beijing's top economic officials, agreed that China would have to do make more concessions before it could join the WTO.
But he said the 15-member EU would stand by the strategy of negotiating an initial package of commitments with the balance to be phased in over an agreed period of time.

"The statement of that structure for entry into the negotiation I personally think would be very helpful on the basis of the discussions I've had with the Chinese," Brittan, who negotiates on trade matters on behalf of the EU, said.

The Brussels-based Commission, the EU's executive arm, has suggested that a downpayment by China on joining the WTO might include a serious tariff-cutting offer, an end to the state's virtual monopoly on external trade and tighter protection of intellectual property.
